# firestore-go vs Google Cloud Firestore emulator

Comparison date: **2026-10-20**. Audience: developers choosing a local Firestore test environment. Engine source reviewed: `a0273a5`. **firestore-go is in development; broad release qualification remains open.**

firestore-go extends local testing beyond successful document operations: applications can exercise required indexes, index builds, TTL deletion, retained history, recovery APIs and optimistic transaction conflicts. These additions are useful for finding configuration and lifecycle failures before deploying to Firestore. They are bounded local implementations, with the evidence and limits below.

Google distributes the same Firestore emulator through gcloud and the Firebase Local Emulator Suite. This comparison distinguishes current official documentation from this repository's measured **Java 1.22.0** reference. That pinned version is not asserted to be Google's latest version. [Google emulator guide][G] · [Firebase emulator guide][F] · [reference lock][lock]

## Side-by-side features

This overview is for orientation; the individual rows in the next section supply the counts.

| High-level capability | Google emulator | firestore-go | Practical value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Application data and realtime APIs | SDK, REST, transactions, listeners and Rules testing | Bounded local implementations of these surfaces | Reuse actual application clients; broad SDK qualification remains open |
| Index-sensitive application tests | Documented composite-index enforcement gap | Production profile checks coverage and uses materialized indexes | Detect missing indexes locally |
| Index lifecycle and Explain | Explain rejected by pinned Java; broader Admin behavior needs separate checks | Production builds, staging, quotas and Explain | Exercise pending/failed configuration and inspect actual local query work |
| Expiry and historical reads | Pinned-reference differences documented; current Google TTL/PITR support not established here | Production TTL and durable PITR | Test expiration effects and historical-read boundaries |
| Recovery workflows | Firebase provides emulator import/export | Configured engine checkpoints, scheduled local backups and restore | Rehearse native recovery; formats are not interchangeable |
| Concurrency modes | Google documents simplified locking | Production optimistic and pessimistic modes | Test contention, changed read sets and atomic aborts |
| Rules development | Official emulator Rules tools and Suite integration | Rules evaluator plus bounded production Rules REST controls | Test Rules deployment and isolated source evaluation |
| Runtime and embedding | Java server; Firebase CLI supplies Suite tooling | Go process and public in-process engine API | Embed host identity, lifecycle and durable state |
| Wider Firebase ecosystem | Official UI and automatic Functions emulator integration | Separate LocalCloud host integration | Different integration paths; no Firebase Suite replacement claim |

## Reading the markers

- **√** — the narrowly named behavior is documented or implemented with linked local evidence. It does **not** mean full Firestore, SDK, API-field or production equivalence.
- **△** — only part of the named behavior is implemented or tested; the row states the boundary.
- **X** — the named behavior is absent in the stated scope. A pinned Java rejection applies to **1.22.0**, not every future Google version.
- **?** — not established by the sources inspected. Silence in Google's documentation never earns X.
- **—** — not applicable to that implementation or counting unit.

**Go default** means Java compatibility behavior. **Go production** means opt-in production corrections, not suitability for production deployment. Both can use configured `Open` engines; disk persistence, Admin APIs and durable workers require that configuration. The standalone `cmd/firestore-go` currently constructs an in-memory `New`/`NewProduction` engine: selecting `--compatibility-profile=production` alone does **not** enable disk persistence or the configured Admin service. See [embedding][embed] and the [CLI source](../cmd/firestore-go/main.go).

In the Google column, [G]/[F] denote current official documentation; repository reports identify pinned Java observations. A Go default-profile result is never treated as a new Google measurement. The tables separate individual behaviors even when they share an RPC or evidence packet.

## Metrics and complete inventory

The [generated metrics](emulator-comparison-metrics.md) count √ / △ / X / ? / — for each checklist column and list only directly supported differences against Google. **A ? never counts as a Google gap.** Default-to-production additions are counted separately, so an intentional Go profile change cannot be presented as proof that Google lacks the feature.

The [complete inventory appendix](emulator-comparison-inventory.md) lists **every existing inventory ID individually**, including each RPC, REST method, protobuf field/enum, Rules signature/property, Pipeline function/overload, Mongo entry and Datastore entry. The [CSV](../parity/emulator-comparison.csv) adds verification labels and evidence paths for filtering. It preserves canonical states from [features.json][inventory]; it does not silently promote historical partial/missing/unassessed rows. Google is ? in this appendix because the production inventory does not contain a corresponding per-ID Google-emulator assessment. The curated checklist above supplies the comparison where evidence exists.

**1,633 inventory entries are not 1,633 independent features.** They include 29 baseline entries and 1,604 production-assessment entries with overlapping counting units. Source discovery is explicitly incomplete. The existing global source-binding audit is stale, so neither the appendix nor its totals establish current full-runtime or production parity. Current bounded implementation reports take precedence for the narrowly described checklist behaviors; their historical packets retain their original scope.

Regenerate and check without network access:

```sh
python3 -B tools/emulator-comparison.py
python3 -B tools/emulator-comparison.py --check
```

This updates only the comparison appendix, CSV and metrics. It never rewrites the production inventory, source hashes, acceptance states or historical matrix.

## Measured size, startup and memory

There are historical paired measurements, but **no new performance benchmark was run for this comparison**. On the recorded 2026-10-17 macOS ARM64 workload, the Go artifact was 18.91 MB versus the Java JAR's 136.71 MB (excluding the JRE); observed child RSS was 30.0–30.2 MiB versus 278.1–279.1 MiB; readiness including polling was 54.7–56.5 ms versus 1,105–1,155 ms. Those measurements bind old Go source `78b7428`, 100 small documents and a single client. They do not measure this revision, packaged images, peak memory or production throughput. Use the [benchmark report][bench] for full inputs, request medians and reproduction commands.

Only reassess the canonical inventory under its existing behavioral-review policy. Recheck Google documentation when updating Google claims; rerun the pinned oracle before expanding a measured version-specific claim. Keep source tests, SDK runs, host integration, images, publication, benchmarks and release qualification separate.
